```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.path = "figures/")
```

## Overview

This simulation compares a single sample to the sampling distributions of the mean and standard deviation, built from 1,000 samples of 100 adult ages. Because the population is known (a discrete uniform distribution of ages 18–114, with μ = 66 and σ = 28), it shows directly how much more accurate the sampling distribution is than a single sample.

## Setup and simulated data

```{r libraries}
library(knitr)    # kable() for formatted tables
library(mosaic)   # favstats() for descriptive statistics
library(dplyr)    # mutate() and select()
library(ggplot2)  # histograms and normal curve overlays

seedValue <- 605
set.seed(seedValue)

# 1,000 samples (columns) of 100 ages (rows), drawn uniformly from 18-114
dataMatrix <- matrix(
  sample(18:114, 100 * 1000, replace = TRUE),
  nrow = 100,
  ncol = 1000
)

df <- data.frame(dataMatrix)
```

This dataset consists of `r ncol(df)` sample sets of `r nrow(df)` observations each.

### Helper functions

```{r helpers}
skewness <- function(x) {
  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^1.5
}

kurtosis <- function(x) {
  mean((x - mean(x))^4) / mean((x - mean(x))^2)^2 - 3
}

describeVar <- function(x) {
  favstats(x) |>
    mutate(
      IQR      = Q3 - Q1,
      Skewness = skewness(x),
      Kurtosis = kurtosis(x)
    ) |>
    select(n, Min = min, Q1, Median = median, Q3, Max = max,
           Mean = mean, SD = sd, IQR, Skewness, Kurtosis) |>
    as_tibble()
}

statNames <- c("n", "Min", "Q1", "Median", "Q3", "Max", "Mean", "SD",
               "IQR", "Skewness", "Excess Kurtosis")

fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)

plotSamplingDist <- function(values, mainTitle, xLabel) {
  valMean  <- mean(values)
  valSD    <- sd(values)
  valN     <- length(values)
  binWidth <- diff(range(values)) / 30  # 30 equal-width bins

  normalCount <- function(x) {
    dnorm(x, mean = valMean, sd = valSD) * valN * binWidth
  }

  ggplot(data.frame(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
    geom_histogram(
      binwidth = binWidth,
      boundary = min(values),
      fill     = "steelblue",
      color    = "white"
    ) +
    geom_function(fun = normalCount, color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = valMean, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
      title    = mainTitle,
      subtitle = paste0("Red curve: normal distribution with the same mean ",
                        "and SD. Dashed line: mean = ", fmt(valMean), "."),
      x        = xLabel,
      y        = "Frequency"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}
```

## 1. Single sample analysis

```{r single-sample}
singleSample <- df$X1
singleStats  <- describeVar(singleSample)

kable(
  singleStats,
  digits    = 2,
  col.names = statNames,
  caption   = "Descriptive Statistics of Age for a Single Sample (X1)"
)
```

```{r single-sample-histogram}
ggplot(df, aes(x = X1)) +
  geom_histogram(
    breaks = seq(17.5, 114.5, length.out = 11),
    fill   = "steelblue",
    color  = "white"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = singleStats$Mean,
    color      = "firebrick",
    linetype   = "dashed",
    linewidth  = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 110, by = 10)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Distribution of Age in a Single Sample (n = 100)",
    subtitle = paste0("Dashed line: mean = ", fmt(singleStats$Mean), " years"),
    x        = "Age (Years)",
    y        = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The ages in this single sample (*n* = 100) ranged from `r singleStats$Min` to `r singleStats$Max` years, spanning the full possible range, and the mean (*M* = `r fmt(singleStats$Mean)`) was slightly below the median (*Mdn* = `r fmt(singleStats$Median)`), with a skewness of `r fmt(singleStats$Skewness)` indicating a nearly symmetric distribution. Instead of a bell-shaped normal pattern, the histogram showed a flat distribution with no dominant peak, and the negative excess kurtosis (`r fmt(singleStats$Kurtosis)`) affirmed a platykurtic, roughly uniform shape with light tails. There was also great variability, with a standard deviation of `r fmt(singleStats$SD)` years and an interquartile range of `r fmt(singleStats$IQR)` years, meaning the middle 50% of ages fell between `r fmt(singleStats$Q1)` and `r fmt(singleStats$Q3)` years.

## 2. Sampling distribution of the mean

```{r sampling-dist-mean}
sampleMeans <- apply(X = df, MARGIN = 2, FUN = mean)
dfMeans     <- data.frame(sampleMeans)

meanStats <- describeVar(dfMeans$sampleMeans)

kable(
  meanStats,
  digits    = 2,
  col.names = statNames,
  caption   = "Descriptive Statistics of the Sampling Distribution of the Mean"
)

seMean   <- sd(dfMeans$sampleMeans)
seSingle <- sd(singleSample) / sqrt(length(singleSample))

cat("Standard error (SD of the sampling distribution of the mean):",
    round(seMean, 4), "\n")
cat("Estimated standard error from the single sample (s / sqrt(n)):",
    round(seSingle, 4), "\n")
```

```{r sampling-dist-mean-histogram}
plotSamplingDist(
  dfMeans$sampleMeans,
  mainTitle = "Sampling Distribution of the Mean Age\n(1,000 Samples, n = 100 Each)",
  xLabel    = "Sample Mean Age (Years)"
)
```

The sampling distribution of the mean, consisting of `r format(nrow(dfMeans), big.mark = ",")` sample means, was unimodal and nearly normal, with skewness (`r fmt(meanStats$Skewness)`) and excess kurtosis (`r fmt(meanStats$Kurtosis)`) both close to zero and a mean (*M* = `r fmt(meanStats$Mean)`) approximately equal to its median (*Mdn* = `r fmt(meanStats$Median)`). The standard deviation of the sample means, which is also the standard error (*SE* = `r fmt(seMean)`), was about one tenth of the single-sample standard deviation and closely approximated the slightly larger formula-based estimate of *s*/√*n* = `r fmt(seSingle)`, with every sample mean falling between `r fmt(meanStats$Min)` and `r fmt(meanStats$Max)` years. As the central limit theorem predicts, averaging 100 observations per sample transformed a population with a flat, uniform distribution into a bell-shaped distribution of sample means tightly clustered around the population mean.

## 3. Sampling distribution of the standard deviation

```{r sampling-dist-sd}
sampleSDs <- apply(X = df, MARGIN = 2, FUN = sd)
dfSDs     <- data.frame(sampleSDs)

sdStats <- describeVar(dfSDs$sampleSDs)

kable(
  sdStats,
  digits    = 2,
  col.names = statNames,
  caption   = "Descriptive Statistics of the Sampling Distribution of the SD"
)
```

```{r sampling-dist-sd-histogram}
plotSamplingDist(
  dfSDs$sampleSDs,
  mainTitle = "Sampling Distribution of the Standard Deviation of Age\n(1,000 Samples, n = 100 Each)",
  xLabel    = "Sample Standard Deviation of Age (Years)"
)
```

The sampling distribution of the standard deviation was unimodal and approximately normal, with a mean (*M* = `r fmt(sdStats$Mean)`) and median (*Mdn* = `r fmt(sdStats$Median)`) that were about the same. It also had a slight negative skew (`r fmt(sdStats$Skewness)`) and excess kurtosis close to zero (`r fmt(sdStats$Kurtosis)`). Sample standard deviations ranged from `r fmt(sdStats$Min)` to `r fmt(sdStats$Max)` years with little spread (*SD* = `r fmt(sdStats$SD)`), which means that any random sample of 100 adults shows a similar level of variation in age. This tight clustering implies that the mean of the sample standard deviations is a steady estimate of the population standard deviation.

## 4. Conclusion

The sampling distribution of the mean yielded a more accurate estimate of the true population mean than the single-sample estimate. The single sample had a mean age of `r fmt(singleStats$Mean)` years (*SD* = `r fmt(singleStats$SD)`, *SE* = `r fmt(seSingle)`) with a 95% CI [`r fmt(singleStats$Mean - qt(0.975, df = 99) * seSingle)`, `r fmt(singleStats$Mean + qt(0.975, df = 99) * seSingle)`], an interval about `r round(2 * qt(0.975, df = 99) * seSingle)` years wide, showing that any one sample of 100 is subject to considerable sampling error. The sampling distribution, in contrast, averaged `r format(nrow(dfMeans), big.mark = ",")` different sample means, so random overestimates and underestimates cancelled out. The standard error of the grand mean decreased to only `r fmt(seMean / sqrt(nrow(dfMeans)), 3)` years (*SE*/√1,000). Based on the sampling distributions, the population mean age is estimated at `r fmt(meanStats$Mean)` years and the population standard deviation at `r fmt(sdStats$Mean)` years. These estimates were similar to the actual parameters of the simulated discrete uniform population of ages 18–114 (μ = 66, σ = 28), with the sampling-distribution estimate of the mean differing from μ by only `r fmt(abs(meanStats$Mean - 66))` years, compared with `r fmt(abs(singleStats$Mean - 66))` years for the single sample.
